At least as of 2024[update], Ethiopia is one of the most rapidly urbanising countries in the world, although its population is still largely rural.[288]

Rural and urban life

Main article: Rural flight in Ethiopia

Migration to urban areas is usually motivated by the hope of better lives. In peasant associations, daily life is a struggle to survive. About 16% of the population in Ethiopia lives on less than one dollar[clarification needed] per day (2008). Only 65% of rural households in Ethiopia consume the World Health Organization's (WHO's) minimum standard of food per day (2,200 kcal), with 42% of children under five years old being underweight.[289]

Most poor families (75%) share their sleeping quarters with livestock, and 40% of children sleep on the floor, where nighttime temperatures average 5 degrees Celsius in the cold season.[289] The average family size is six or seven, living in a 30 square metre mud and thatch hut, with less than two hectares of land to cultivate.[289]

The peasant associations face a cycle of poverty. Since the landholdings are so small, farmers cannot allow the land to lie fallow, which reduces soil fertility.[289] This land degradation reduces the production of fodder for livestock, which causes low milk yields.[289] Since the community burns livestock manure as fuel, rather than plowing the nutrients back into the land, the crop production is reduced.[289] The low productivity of agriculture leads to inadequate incomes for farmers, hunger, malnutrition and disease. These unhealthy farmers have difficulty working the land and the productivity drops further.[289]

Although conditions are drastically better in cities, all of Ethiopia suffers from poverty and poor sanitation. However, poverty in Ethiopia fell from 44% to 29.6% during 2000–2011, according to the World Bank.[290] In the capital city of Addis Ababa, 55% of the population used to live in slums.[285] However, a construction boom in both the private and the public sector has led to a dramatic improvement in living standards in major cities, particularly in Addis Ababa. Notably, government-built condominium housing complexes have sprung up throughout the city, benefiting close to 600,000 individuals.[291] Sanitation is the most pressing need in the city, with most of the population lacking access to waste treatment facilities. This contributes to the spread of illness through unhealthy water.[285]

Despite the urban living conditions, residents of Addis Ababa are more financially secure than those living in peasant associations, owing to their increased educational and economic opportunities. Unlike rural children, 69% of urban children are enrolled in primary school, and 35% are eligible to attend secondary school.[clarification needed][285] Addis Ababa has its own university as well as its own secondary schools. The literacy rate in Addis Ababa is 82% as of 2008.[285]

Many NGOs are working to solve this problem; however, most are far apart, uncoordinated, and working in isolation. The Sub-Saharan Africa NGO Consortium is attempting to coordinate efforts.

Languages

Main article: Languages of Ethiopia
Languages of Ethiopia as of 2007[update] Census:[6]
  1. Oromo (33.8%)
  2. Amharic (29.3%)
  3. Somali (6.20%)
  4. Tigrinya (5.90%)
  5. Sidamo (4.00%)
  6. Wolaytta (2.20%)
  7. Gurage (2.00%)
  8. Afar (1.70%)
  9. Hadiyya (1.70%)
  10. Gamo (1.50%)
  11. Other languages (11.7%)

According to Glottolog, there are 109 languages spoken in Ethiopia, while Ethnologue lists 90 individual languages spoken in the country.[292][293] Most people in the country speak Afroasiatic languages of the Cushitic or Semitic branches. The former includes the Oromo language, spoken by the Oromo, and Somali, spoken by the Somalis; the latter includes Amharic, spoken by the Amhara, and Tigrinya, spoken by the Tigrayans. Together, these four groups make up about three-quarters of Ethiopia's population. Other Afroasiatic languages with a significant number of speakers include the Cushitic Sidamo, Afar, Hadiyya and Agaw languages, as well as the Semitic Gurage languages, Harari, Silt'e, and Argobba languages.[6] Arabic, which also belongs to the Afroasiatic family, is likewise spoken in some areas.[294]

English is the most widely spoken foreign language, the medium of instruction in secondary schools and all tertiary education; federal laws are also published in British English in the Federal Negarit Gazeta including the 1995 constitution.[295]

Amharic was once the language of primary school instruction, but has been replaced in many areas by regional languages such as Oromo, Somali or Tigrinya.[296] All languages enjoy equal state recognition in the 1995 Constitution of Ethiopia.[144]

Script

Ethiopia's principal orthography is the Ge'ez script. Employed as an abugida for several of the country's languages, it first came into usage in the 6th and 5th centuries BC as an abjad to transcribe the Semitic Ge'ez language.[297] Ge'ez now serves as the liturgical language of both the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Churches. During the 1980s, the Ethiopic character set was computerised. It is today part of the Unicode standard as Ethiopic, Ethiopic Extended, Ethiopic Supplement, and Ethiopic Extended-A.

Other writing systems have also been used over the years by different Ethiopian communities. The latter include Bakri Sapalo's script for Oromo.[298]

Religion

Main article: Religion in Ethiopia
Religions in Ethiopia (Afrobarometer 2023 survey):[299]
  1. Orthodox (40.1%)
  2. Protestant (22.1%)
  3. Catholic (0.50%)
  4. Muslim (36.9%)
  5. African traditional religions (0.20%)
  6. None (0.10%)
  7. Other (0.10%)

According to the 2007 National Census, Christians make up 62.8% of the country's population, Muslims 33.9%, practitioners of traditional faiths 2.6%, and other religions 0.6%.[6] The ratio of the Christian to Muslim population has largely remained stable when compared to previous censuses.[300] Sunnis form the majority of Muslims with non-denominational Muslims being the second largest group of Muslims, and the Shia are a minority. Sunnis are largely Shafi'is or Salafis; there are also many Sufis there.[301]

Ethiopia has close historical ties with all three of the world's major Abrahamic religions. In the 4th century, the Ethiopian empire was one of the first in the world to officially adopt Christianity as the state religion. As a result of the resolutions of the Council of Chalcedon, in 451 the Miaphysites, which included the vast majority of Christians in Egypt and Ethiopia, were accused of monophysitism and designated as heretics under the common name of Coptic Christianity.[d][302]

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is part of Oriental Orthodoxy. It is by far the largest Christian denomination, although a number of P'ent'ay (Protestant) churches have recently gained ground. Since 1930, a relatively small Ethiopian Catholic Church has existed in full communion with Rome, with adherents making up less than 1% of the total population.[300]

Islam in Ethiopia dates back to the founding of the religion in 622 when a group of Muslims were counselled by Muhammad to escape persecution in Mecca. The disciples subsequently migrated to Abyssinia via modern-day Eritrea, which was at the time ruled by Ashama ibn-Abjar, a pious Christian emperor.[303]

Health

Main articles: Health in Ethiopia and Healthcare in Ethiopia

Only a minority of Ethiopians are born in hospitals, while most are born in rural households. Those who are expected to give birth at home have elderly women serve as midwives who assist with the delivery.[304] The WHO estimates that "a majority of maternal fatalities and disabilities could be prevented if deliveries were to take place at well-equipped health centres, with adequately trained staff".[305] Birth rates, infant mortality rates, and death rates are lower in cities than in rural areas due to better access to education, medicines, and hospitals.[285] Life expectancy is better in cities compared to rural areas, but there have been significant improvements witnessed throughout the country as of 2016, the average Ethiopian living to be 62.2 years old, according to a UNDP report.[306] Despite sanitation being a problem, use of improved water sources is also on the rise; 81% in cities compared to 11% in rural areas.

Ethiopia's main health problems are said to be communicable (contagious) diseases worsened by poor sanitation and malnutrition. Over 58 M people (nearly half the population) do not have access to clean water as of 2023[update].[307] These problems are exacerbated by the shortage of trained doctors and nurses and health facilities.[308] The WHO's 2006 World Health Report gives a figure of 1,936 physicians (for 2003), which comes to about 2.6 per 100,000.[309]

The National Mental Health Strategy, published in 2012, introduced the development of policy designed to improve mental health care in Ethiopia. This strategy mandated that mental health be integrated into the primary health care system.[310] However, the success of the National Mental Health Strategy has been limited. For example, the burden of depression is estimated to have increased 34.2% from 2007 to 2017.[311] Furthermore, the prevalence of stigmatising attitudes, inadequate leadership and co-ordination of efforts, as well as a lack of mental health awareness in the general population, all remain as obstacles to successful mental health care.[312]

In the 2024 Global Hunger Index (GHI), Ethiopia ranks 102nd out of 127 countries and has a score of 26.2, which indicates a serious level of hunger.[313]

Education

Main article: Education in Ethiopia
See also: Higher education in Ethiopia

The current system follows school expansion schemes which are very similar to the system in the rural areas during the 1980s, with an addition of deeper regionalisation, providing rural education in students' own languages starting at the elementary level, and with more budgetary financing allocated to the education sector. Public education is free at primary levels and usually offers between age 7 and 12. The sequence of general education in Ethiopia is six years of primary school, then four years of lower secondary school followed by two years of higher secondary school.[314]

Ethiopian education is governed by the Ministry of Education and uses a 4+4+2+2 system; elementary education consists of eight years, divided into two cycles of four years, and four years of secondary education, divided into two stages of two years.[315] National exams are conducted by the National Educational Assessment and Examination Agency (NEAEA). Since 2018, there are two national exams: the Ethiopian General Secondary Education Certificate Examination (EGSECE), also known as the Grade 10 national exam, and the Grade 12 national exam.[316]

As of 2022[update], there are 83 universities, 42 public universities, and more than 35 higher education institutions. Foreign students constitute 16,305 in higher education level. The overall number of tertiary students in both public and private institutions exploded by more than 2,000%, from 34,000 in 1991 to 757,000 in 2014, per UIS data.[317][318] Access to education in Ethiopia has improved significantly. Approximately three million people were enrolled in primary school in 1994–95, but by 2008–09, primary enrolment had risen to 15.5 million – an increase of over 500%.[319] In 2013–14, there was a significant boost in gross enrolment across all regions.[320] The national GER was 104.8% for boys, 97.8% for girls and 101.3% across both sexes.[321]

The literacy rate has increased in recent years: according to the 1994 census, the literacy rate in Ethiopia was 23.4%.[293] In 2007 it was estimated to be 39% (male 49.1% and female 28.9%).[322] A report by UNDP in 2011 showed that the literacy rate in Ethiopia was 46.7%. The same report also indicated that the female literacy rate had increased from 27 to 39% from 2004 to 2011, and the male literacy rate had increased from 49 to 59% over the same period for persons 10 years and older.[323] By 2015, the literacy rate had further increased, to 49.1% (57.2% male and 41.1% female).[324]

Culture

Main article: Culture of Ethiopia

The culture of Ethiopia is diverse, formed by the interaction of Semitic, Cushitic and less populous Nilo-Saharan speaking peoples since the first millennium BCE. The dominant Semitic-speaking groups, such as the Tigrayans, Amharas and Gurage, are distinguished by their feudal traditions, hierarchical structure and agrarian life. This is rooted partly in South Arabian culture as a result of return migration, while the southern Cushitic (Oromo and Somali) are strong adherents to egalitarianism and pastoral life. Other traditions from the Kafficho, Sidamo, and Afar peoples are also present.[325]

Holidays

Main article: Public holidays in Ethiopia

The government of Ethiopia recognises 6 patriotic and public holidays and 9 major religious holidays. The year (Gregorian calendar) starts with Ethiopian Christmas on 7 January. Timkat ('Epiphany'), celebrated on 19 or 20 January, marks the baptism of Jesus Christ by John the Baptist. Timkat is recognised by the United Nations as part of its "Intangible Cultural Heritage Lists" which designate important cultural and religious holidays.[326][327] Three holidays are movable: Ramadan, Good Friday and Easter, two of which are always in spring and one of which (Ramadan) may occur at any time of year. Other holidays include Mawlid, which begins on the 12th or 17th day of the third month of the Islamic calendar depending on the denomination of the celebrants. The majority of Ethiopian Muslims are Sunni, thus it is celebrated on the 12th day. Other Islamic holidays include Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha. Meskel is a Christian holiday celebrating the discovery of the True Cross. Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha are trans-national holidays celebrated across the Islamic world, while Meskel is also celebrated in Eritrea[328] and by Eritrean and Ethiopian diaspora communities abroad,[329][330] but it is most prominent in Ethiopia.[331][332][e]

The first public holiday of the Gregorian calendar year is Adwa Victory Day on 2 March, commemorating Emperor Menelik II's victory over the colonisation efforts of Italy in 1896. Others are International Workers' Day on the 1st of May, the Ethiopian Patriots' Victory Day for celebrating the return of Emperor Haile Selassie and thus the liberation of fascist Italian occupation on the 5th of May, and the Downfall of the Derg on the 28th of May, a recent holiday promoted to public status after 1991. The most prominent public holiday is Enkutatash (Ethiopian new year celebration) on 11 or 12 September. Defence Day, on the 26th of October, celebrates servicemen, and is the last holiday in the Gregorian calendar.[337]

Various other festivals and holidays are celebrated across the country, including Irreechaa celebrated by the Oromo community.[338][f]

Art and architecture

Main articles: Ethiopian art; Architecture of Ethiopia; List of castles in Ethiopia; and Rock-Hewn Churches, Lalibela

Ethiopian arts were largely influenced by Christian iconography throughout much of their history, such as illuminated manuscripts, painting, crosses, icons and other metalwork such as crowns. Most historical arts were commissioned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, the state religion for a millennium. Earlier Aksumite period art was most prominently stone carvings as evidenced in their stelae, though there is no surviving Christian art from this era. As Christianity was introduced, its iconography was partly influenced by Byzantine art. Most remaining artworks beyond the early modern period were ruined as a result of the invasion of the Adal Sultanate in the Ethiopian Highlands, but were revived by Catholic emissaries.[citation needed] The Western intervention in Ethiopian art began in the 20th century, though artists maintained a traditional Ethiopian character in their work. Some notable contemporary Ethiopian artists include Afewerk Tekle, Lemma Guya, Martha Nasibù, Ale Felege Selam, and others.[g]

The "Bete Medhane Alem" or "House of our Saviour" is one of the 12 churches in Lalibela built under Emperor Lalibela I. Emperor Lalibela I commissioned large portions of the Lalibela church complex, and it was named after him. This has been attributed to Christian Ethiopians' desire during medieval times, due to their blockage from Jerusalem by Muslim conquests, to replicate their own "new Jerusalem" at a national level.[341]

Aksumite architecture continued to flourish in the 4th century CE. Aksumite stelae commonly used single blocks and rocks. The Tomb of the False Door, built for Aksumite emperors, used the monolithic style.[342] The Lalibela civilisation was largely influenced by Aksumite architecture, but the layer of stones or wood is quite different for some dwellings.[343]

In the Gondarine period, the architecture of Ethiopia was influenced by Baroque, Arab, Turkish and Gujarati Indian styles independently taught by Portuguese emissaries in the 16th and 17th centuries.[citation needed] One example is the imperial fortress Fasil Ghebbi, which is influenced by a mix of these styles. Medieval architecture also influenced architecture of the later 19th- and 20th-century era.[344]

Literature

Main articles: Ethiopian literature and Ethiopian philosophy

Ethiopian literature traces back to the Aksumite period in the 4th century, mostly religious motifs. In royal inscriptions, it employed both Ge'ez and Greek, but the latter was discontinued in 350.[citation needed] Unlike most Sub-Saharan African countries, Ethiopia has an ancient distinct language, Ge'ez, which dominated politics and education, In spite of the current political instability in the country endangering the cultural heritage of these works, preservation has improved in recent years.[345]

During the Middle Ages, composers such as Abba Gorgoryos and Giyorgis of Segla made lasting contributions to Ethiopian languages, such as writing the earliest dictionaries of Amharic and Ge'ez, as well as composing religious hymns and doctrinal justifications of issues in the Ethiopian Orthodox church and practices.[346][347]

Ethiopian literary works in this period mostly consisted of handwritten codexes (Amharic: ብራና, romanised: branna). Branna are prepared by gathering parchment leaves and sewing them together. The size may vary considerably depending on the number of volumes and manner of preparation. For example, a pocket size codex is 45 cm in length, but are heavier in weight. Historians have speculated that archaic codexes existed in Ethiopia.[citation needed] Today manuscripts resembling primitive codexes are still used where parchment leaves are convenient for writing.[345]

Another notable form of writing is the protective (or magic) scroll. Some of these were intended for magical purposes, such as the ketab, which is used for magical defence. Scrolls were typically produced by debtera, non-ordained clerical experts on exorcism and healings. Scrolls could range in size from the portable 30 cm scroll, to the 2 cm size,[clarification needed] which is often unrolled and hung on the walls of houses. Scrolls being the original medium for Ethiopia literature is highly disputed, as there is overwhelming evidence that Ge'ez language books were written in codex form.[citation needed] Ethiopians also used accordion books (called sensul) in the late 15th and 16th century, made of folded parchment paper, with or without a cover. These books usually contain pictorial representations of the life and death of religious figures, juxtaposed with other significant texts.[345]

Baalu Girma (1939–1984), novelist and critic; author of The End[348]
Haddis Alemayehu (1910–2003), foreign minister and novelist; author of Love to the Grave[349]

Baalu Girma and Haddis Alemayehu have been noted as the most influential novelists in Ethiopian history. Girma has critiqued the communist government in the 80s in Ethiopia in his works. Haddis Alemayehu wrote one of the first examinations of realism, as well as a romantic tragedy novel, and influenced the Ethiopian intellectual community.[350][351]

Poetry is popular in Ethiopia. Most poets recount past events, social unrests, poverty and famine. Qene is the most used element of Ethiopian poetry – it is regarded as a form of Amharic poetry, though the term may also refer to any poem. The defining characteristic of qene is sem-ena-werq (Amharic: ሰምና ወርቅ, romanised: säməna wärq, lit. 'wax and gold'), a literary device where two metaphorical words, one with an obvious meaning (wax) and the other more obscure (the gold), are paired to layer hidden meanings within the text.[352] The most notable poets are Tsegaye Gebre-Medhin,[353] Kebede Michael and Mengistu Lemma.[354]

Ethiopian philosophy has been superlatively prolific since ancient times in Africa, though strongly influenced by Greek and Patristic philosophy. The best known philosophical revival was in the early modern period, such as Zera Yacob (1599–1692) and his student Walda Heywat, who wrote Hatata (Inquiry) in 1667 as an argument for the existence of God.

Music

Main article: Music of Ethiopia
See also: Ethiopian Golden Age of music

The music of Ethiopia is extremely diverse, with each of the country's 80 ethnic groups being associated with unique sounds. Ethiopian music uses a distinct modal system that is pentatonic, with characteristically long intervals between some notes. As with many other aspects of Ethiopian culture and tradition, tastes in music and lyrics are strongly linked with those in neighbouring Eritrea, Somalia, Djibouti, and Sudan.[355][356] Traditional singing in Ethiopia presents diverse styles of polyphony (heterophony, drone, imitation, and counterpoint). Traditionally, lyricism in Ethiopian songwriting is strongly associated with views of patriotism or national pride, romance, friendship, and a unique type of memoire known as tizita.

Saint Yared, a 6th-century Aksumite composer, is widely regarded as the father of the traditional music of Eritrea and Ethiopia, creating liturgical music of the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Churches.[357]

Modern music traces back to the reign of Emperor Haile Selassie, when 40 Armenian orphans called Arba Lijoch arrived from Jerusalem to Addis Ababa. By 1924, the band had become Ethiopia's first official orchestra, but after World War II, several similar bands emerged, such as the Imperial Bodyguard Band, Army Band, and Police Band.[358]

In the 1960s and 1970s, traditional-style modern Ethiopian music was revived in what is known as the "Golden Age". Several notable musical artists emerged thereafter, such as Tilahun Gessesse, Alemayehu Eshete, Bizunesh Bekele, Muluken Melesse, and Mahmoud Ahmed. These artists also employed the traditional style called tizita. During the Derg regime, these artists were prohibited to perform in the country and often forced into exile in North America and Europe, causing them to incorporate jazz and funk influences. Musicians of this style include Roha Band, Walias Band, and Ethio Stars. By this time, Neway Debebe was critical of the Derg government.[352]

Modern music developed further in the 1990s and 2000s. In this period, the most popular artists were Aster Aweke, Gigi and Teddy Afro. Ethiopian music further modernised in the next decade. DJ Rophnan was renowned for pioneering EDM in the country after releasing his debut album Reflection in 2018.[352]

Calendar

Main articles: Ethiopian calendar and Oromo calendar

Ethiopia has several local calendars. The most widely known is the Ethiopian calendar, also known as the Ge'ez calendar, and written with the ancient Ge'ez script, one of the oldest alphabets still in use in the world.[359] It is based on the older Alexandrian or Coptic calendar, which in turn derives from the Egyptian calendar. Like the Coptic calendar, the Ethiopian calendar has twelve months of exactly 30 days each plus five or six epagomenal days, which form a thirteenth month. The Ethiopian months begin on the same days as those of the Coptic calendar, but their names are in Ge'ez.[360]

Like the Julian calendar, the sixth epagomenal day—which in essence is a leap day—is added every four years without exception on 29 August of the Julian calendar, six months before the Julian leap day. Thus, the first day of the Ethiopian year, 1 Mäskäräm, for years between 1901 and 2099 (inclusive), is usually 11 September (Gregorian), but falls on 12 September in years before the Gregorian leap year. It is approximately seven years and three months behind the Gregorian calendar because of an alternate calculation in determining the date of the Annunciation of Jesus.[361]

Another calendrical system was developed around 300 BC by the Oromo people. A lunar-stellar calendar, this Oromo calendar relies on astronomical observations of the moon in conjunction with seven particular stars or constellations. The Oromo months (stars/lunar phases) are Bittottessa (Iangulum), Camsa (Pleiades), Bufa (Aldebarran), Waxabajjii (Belletrix), Obora Gudda (Central Orion-Saiph), Obora Dikka (Sirius), Birra (full moon), Cikawa (gibbous moon), Sadasaa (quarter moon), Abrasa (large crescent), Ammaji (medium crescent), and Gurrandala (small crescent).[362]

Media

Main articles: Communications in Ethiopia and Media in Ethiopia

The Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), formerly known as ETV, is a state-owned public service broadcaster. Radio broadcasting began in 1935, and television service began in 1962 with the assistance of British firm Thomson and Emperor Haile Selassie.[3] Since 2015, EBC has upgraded its studios with modernised transmission.

Kana TV is the most popular TV channel in Ethiopia.[363] It is mainly known for dubbing foreign content into Amharic. For several decades, EBC served as the main source for mass media until the late 2000s, when EBS TV launched as the first private television channel. Moreover, numerous private channels were founded in 2016, contributing to the growth of privately owned media companies in the country. Fana TV has been the largest TV network since its launch in 2017.

The most widely circulated newspapers in Ethiopia are Addis Fortune, Capital Ethiopia, Ethiopian Reporter, Addis Zemen (in Amharic), and Ethiopian Herald.[364]

The sole internet service provider is the national telecommunications firm Ethio telecom. A large portion of users in the country access the internet through mobile devices.[365] As of July 2016[update], there are around 4.29 million people who have internet access at their home as compared to a quarter of a million users a decade before that.[366] The Ethiopian government has at times intentionally shut down internet service in the country or restricted access to certain social media sites during periods of political unrest. In August 2016, following protests and demonstrations in the Oromia Region, all access to the internet was shut down for a period of two days.[367] In June 2017, the government shut down access to the internet for mobile users during a period that coincided with the administration of university entrance examination. Although the reason for the restriction was not confirmed by the government,[365] the move was similar to a measure taken during the same period in 2016, after a leak of test questions.[368][369]

Cinema

Main article: Cinema of Ethiopia

The first cinema was introduced in 1898, three years after the first world film was projected. Italian minister Federico Ciccodicola [it] offered cinematic artefacts[clarification needed] to Emperor Menelik II. The early 20th century appearance with spectacle was around 1909 and embraced by documentary or biographical films. Au de Menilek was the first film directed by Charles Martel. The first 16mm black-and-white film dedicated to coronation of Emperor Zewditu, then the coronation of Emperor Haile Selassie, was filmed. The 1990s saw an international boom in Ethiopian films. The most influential people in this era were Haile Gerima, Salem Mekuria, Yemane Demissie, and Teshome Gabriel. Films began to be filmed in the Amharic language in the 2000s. The Ethiopian films with the highest international box office grosses include Selanchi, Difret, Lamb, Prince of Love, and Lambadina. The best-known Ethiopian actors include Selam Tesfaye, Fryat Yemane, Hanan Tarik, Mahder Assefa, Amleset Muchie, and Ruth Negga.

One of the most prestigious film awards is the Gumma Film Awards, held in Addis Ababa. The ceremony, which was started in 2014, is broadcast on live television on some stations.[370] Festivals including Addis International Film Festival and the Ethiopian International Film Festival showcase amateur and professional filmmakers' works. They were established in 2007[371] and 2005 respectively.[372]

Cuisine

Main article: Ethiopian cuisine
See also: List of Ethiopian dishes and foods

The best-known Ethiopian cuisine consists of various types of thick meat stews, known as wat in Ethiopian culture, and vegetable side dishes served on top of injera, a large sourdough flatbread made of teff flour. It is not eaten with utensils, but instead the injera is used to scoop up the entrées and side dishes. Almost universally in Ethiopia, it is common to eat from the same dish in the middle of the table with a group of people. It is also a common custom to feed others with one's own hands—a tradition referred to as gursha.[373] Traditional Ethiopian cuisine employs no pork, as it is forbidden in Ethiopian Orthodox Christian and Islamic faiths; Ethiopian Orthodox Christians also fast from meat on Wednesdays, Fridays, and the days leading up to Easter and Christmas.[374]

Chechebsa, marqa, chukko, michirra, and dhanga are the most popular dishes from the Oromo people. Kitfo, which originated among the Gurage people, is another of the country's most popular delicacies. In addition, doro wat (Amharic: ዶሮ ወጥ) and tsebehi derho (Tigrinya: ጽብሒ ድርሆ), are other popular dishes, originating from northwestern Ethiopia.[375] Tihlo (ጥሕሎ), a type of dumpling prepared from roasted barley flour and originating from the Tigray Region, is now very popular in Amhara and spreading further south.[376]

Sport

Main article: Sport in Ethiopia

The main sports in Ethiopia are track and field (particularly long distance running) and football. Ethiopian athletes have won many Olympic gold medals in track and field, most of them in long distance running.[377] Abebe Bikila became the first athlete from a Sub-Saharan country to win an Olympic gold medal when he won the Marathon at the 1960 Rome Olympic Games in a world record time of 2:15:16.[378][379]

The Ethiopia national football team was one of four founding members of the Confederation of African Football and won the Africa Cup of Nations in 1962.[380] Ethiopia has Sub-Saharan Africa's longest basketball tradition, as it established a national basketball team in 1949.[citation needed]
